all-purpose flour.notes: Higher protein; may make baked goods chewier.
Use a blend designed as a direct flour replacement.

baking powder.ratio: 1/4 tsp baking soda + 1/2 tsp cream of tartar per 1 tsp baking powder

baking soda.ratio: 3 tsp baking powder per 1 tsp baking soda
baking soda.notes: Results may differ because baking powder contains its own acid.

bread crumbs.ratio: 3/4 cup cracker crumbs per 1 cup dry breadcrumbs
bread crumbs.notes: Good for coatings, meatloaf, and fillers.
Best for meatloaf or meatballs rather than breading.

brown sugar.ratio: 1 cup sugar + 1/4 cup molasses per 1 cup packed brown sugar

brown sugar.notes: Less moisture and caramel flavor; texture may be crisper.

butter.notes: Stick margarine generally performs better than spreadable tubs in baking.
Works in many recipes but removes butter flavor and changes texture.
Refined coconut oil has less coconut flavor.

butter.ratio: replace up to half of the butter 1:1
butter.notes: Useful for reducing fat in some cakes and quick breads; produces a softer texture.

buttermilk.ratio: 1 tbsp lemon juice plus enough milk to make 1 cup
1 tbsp vinegar plus enough milk to make 1 cup

buttermilk.notes: Adjust milk slightly to reach a buttermilk-like consistency.

cake flour.ratio: 3/4 cup + 2 tbsp AP flour + 2 tbsp cornstarch per 1 cup cake flour

cornstarch.notes: Good for thickening sauces; may produce a less glossy result.

cornstarch.ratio: about 2 tsp arrowroot per 1 tbsp cornstarch
cornstarch.notes: Good for clear sauces; avoid prolonged high heat.

cream of tartar.notes: Useful for stabilizing whipped egg whites.
Useful where acidity is the main function.

egg.ratio: 1 tbsp ground flax + 3 tbsp water per egg
egg.notes: Let sit about 5 minutes. Good for binding in muffins, cookies, and quick breads.

egg.ratio: 1 tbsp chia + 3 tbsp water per egg
egg.notes: Let gel 5-10 minutes. Adds visible seeds unless ground.
Adds moisture; best for cakes, muffins, and quick breads.
Adds moisture and richness; best where egg is not needed primarily for lift.

heavy cream.ratio: 3/4 cup milk + about 1/3 cup melted butter per 1 cup cream
heavy cream.notes: Works for cooking and baking but will not whip like heavy cream.
Good for soups and sauces; lower fat and not suitable for whipping.
Rich non-dairy substitute but may add coconut flavor.

half-and-half.ratio: 3/4 cup whole milk + 1/4 cup heavy cream per 1 cup
half-and-half.notes: Close approximation for cooking and coffee.

honey.notes: Flavor and moisture will differ slightly.

honey.ratio: 1 1/4 cups sugar + 1/4 cup liquid per 1 cup honey
honey.notes: Less honey flavor and may require other recipe adjustments.

maple syrup.notes: Similar sweetness and consistency but distinctly different flavor.
Much stronger flavor, particularly with blackstrap molasses.

milk.ratio: 1/2 cup evaporated milk + 1/2 cup water per 1 cup milk

milk.notes: Neutral and creamy; good general-purpose non-dairy substitute.
Protein content makes it useful in baking.
Thinner than dairy milk and may add a mild nutty flavor.

molasses.notes: Texture is similar but flavor is milder.
Sweeter and much lighter in flavor.

powdered sugar.notes: Blend until very fine and powdery.

self-rising flour.ratio: 1 cup minus 2 tsp AP flour + 1 1/2 tsp baking powder + 1/2 tsp salt

sour cream.notes: One of the closest replacements for dips, baking, and toppings.
Thinner than sour cream but generally works well in baking.
Best in savory applications or baked dishes.

vegetable oil.notes: Neutral flavor and very similar behavior.
Neutral oil suitable for most cooking and baking.
May firm when chilled and may contribute coconut flavor.
Useful in muffins and quick breads when reducing fat.

olive oil.notes: Neutral flavor and suitable for higher-heat cooking.

white wine.notes: Sweeter; add a small splash of vinegar or lemon juice for acidity if appropriate.
Useful in savory dishes where wine is primarily providing liquid.

red wine.notes: Sweeter; add a small amount of vinegar if acidity is needed.
Useful in savory dishes and braises; lacks wine acidity.

rice vinegar.notes: Stronger flavor; a small pinch of sugar can make it closer to seasoned rice vinegar.
Similar acidity with a slightly sharper taste.

apple cider vinegar.notes: Good when acidity is more important than vinegar flavor.

lemon juice.notes: Excellent general substitute with a different citrus flavor.

lemon juice.ratio: about 1/2 tsp vinegar per 1 tsp lemon juice
lemon juice.notes: Best where lemon juice is being used mainly for acidity.

lime juice.notes: Acidity is similar but flavor is distinctly different.

soy sauce.notes: Usually similar flavor and often gluten-free, but check the label.
Sweeter and generally less salty than soy sauce.

worcestershire sauce.notes: Approximation for savory dishes; lacks the full spice and fermented flavor.

dijon mustard.notes: Similar flavor with a coarser texture.

tomato paste.ratio: 3 tbsp tomato sauce per 1 tbsp tomato paste
tomato paste.notes: Simmer or reduce when possible to remove excess water.
Sweeter and seasoned; best only when the flavor fits the dish.

tomato sauce.notes: Adjust thickness and seasoning as needed.
Chunkier texture; blend for a smoother sauce.

chicken broth.ratio: 1 bouillon cube or equivalent base per 1 cup hot water
chicken broth.notes: Salt level varies greatly by brand.
Good general substitute with a lighter flavor.

beef broth.ratio: 1 bouillon cube or equivalent base per 1 cup hot water
beef broth.notes: Check salt before seasoning the finished dish.
Adds savory depth and works particularly well in stews and sauces.

vegetable broth.ratio: prepare according to bouillon package directions

vegetable broth.notes: Use only when a vegetarian result is not required.

garlic.ratio: about 1/8 tsp garlic powder per small garlic clove
garlic.notes: Powder is more concentrated and lacks fresh garlic texture.
Convenient but usually milder than freshly chopped garlic.

fresh ginger.ratio: about 1/4 tsp ground ginger per 1 tbsp fresh ginger
fresh ginger.notes: Ground ginger is warmer and less bright than fresh.

fresh herbs.ratio: 1 tsp dried herbs per 1 tbsp chopped fresh herbs
fresh herbs.notes: Add dried herbs earlier in cooking so they have time to hydrate.

fresh basil.notes: Dried basil is less fresh-tasting; add during cooking rather than at the end.

fresh oregano.notes: Dried oregano is often stronger than fresh.

fresh rosemary.notes: Crush dried rosemary before adding if the pieces are large.

allspice.ratio: 1/2 tsp cinnamon + 1/2 tsp ground cloves per 1 tsp allspice

apple pie spice.ratio: 1/2 tsp cinnamon + 1/4 tsp nutmeg + 1/8 tsp cardamom per 1 tsp
apple pie spice.notes: Useful when a premixed apple pie spice blend is unavailable.

vanilla extract.notes: Not a true vanilla replacement but can provide complementary sweetness and aroma.

yeast.substitute: instant yeast for active dry yeast
yeast.notes: Instant yeast can usually be mixed directly into dry ingredients.

yeast.substitute: active dry yeast for instant yeast
yeast.notes: Active dry yeast may benefit from dissolving or proofing first.
